The Streak-necked flycatcher (Mionectes striaticollis) is a small Tyranid found in the Andean cloud forests, and its life history reflects the energetically conservative strategy typical of many Neotropical passerines. Field records indicate that newly hatched chicks emerge from eggs incubated at a temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], with an incubation period lasting 19 days [ab = 19 days]. This duration is comparable to that of the congeneric Mionectes olivaceus, which provides a basis for estimating the initial wet body mass of the hatchling at 1.99 grams [Ww0 = 1.99 grams], a value that reflects the modest energetic reserves allocated to the altricial nestling at the start of its development. Upon hatching, the chick is entirely dependent on biparental care, and the nestling period is marked by rapid mass gain as the parents deliver a steady supply of arthropod prey.

At the body temperature typical of active thermoregulation in this species (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), the nestling reaches the fledging stage after 18 days since birth [tx = 18 days since birth], a relatively short nestling phase for a bird of this size, likely constrained by high predation pressure in the understory. During this period, the developing chick grows rapidly, progressing from a downy, brooded nestling to a full-feathered fledgling. The transition to independence is a critical stage; once the fledgling leaves the nest, it continues to be provisioned by the parents for a brief interval while it perfects its foraging skills. This accelerated developmental schedule contrasts with longer nestling periods reported for some temperate-dwelling Tyrannidae, highlighting the influence of tropical environmental conditions on the timing of ontogenetic milestones in Mionectes striaticollis.

Sexual maturation in this species proceeds under the same thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], with individuals typically attaining puberty at 54 days since birth [tp = 54 days since birth]. This relatively rapid progression to reproductive maturity is notable among Andean flycatchers and likely reflects selection for early breeding in a seasonal environment with fluctuating resource availability. Nevertheless, the onset of gonadal activity does not immediately translate into reproductive effort; first-year birds often delay breeding until they have secured a territory and established a pair bond. The physiological underpinnings of this maturation process involve the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, triggered by photoperiodic cues and possibly modulated by body condition. Field studies of related species suggest that nutritional status during the post-fledging period plays a key role in determining the exact timing of puberty, although for Mionectes striaticollis the available data point consistently toward the 54-day milestone as a reliable benchmark.

The first successful breeding event for a female Mionectes striaticollis occurs, under optimal conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], at approximately 402 days since birth [tR = approximately 402 days since birth]. This substantial delay between the attainment of puberty and first reproduction suggests that acquiring a high-quality territory and a compatible mate imposes a prolonged period of social maturation. The female typically constructs a pear-shaped, mossy nest with a side entrance, often placed near streams or on steep banks. Her typical clutch consists of two to three eggs [N_R_i = clutch consists of two to three eggs] and she raises a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a modest reproductive output that aligns with the brood size observed in other Mionectes species. This annual rhythm represents the maximum reproductive rate for the species, constrained by the energetic demands of egg production, incubation, and provisioning.

As an adult, the female Streak-necked flycatcher reaches an ultimate wet body mass of 15 grams [Wwi = 15 grams], a value that fits well within the reported range of 13 to 17 grams for the species and places it among the smaller members of the genus.
